items.title: 0.9999... equals 1, exactly
items.claim: The decimal expansion 0.999... (infinitely many 9s) does not approach 1 — it IS 1. Two different decimal expansions can represent the same real number.

options.text: They're approximately equal but slightly different
They have zero difference (1 - 0.999... = 0); 0.999... = sum of 9/10 to the n for n from 1 to infinity = 9/10 / (1 - 1/10) = 1 exactly

items.reveal:
Every infinite decimal expansion is, by definition, a convergent series.
0.999... = 9/10 + 9/100 + 9/1000 + ...
     = 9/10 * (1 + 1/10 + 1/100 + ...)
     = 9/10 * 1/(1 - 1/10)
     = 9/10 * 10/9
     = 1

Another argument: let x = 0.999... Then 10x = 9.999... Subtract: 10x - x = 9.999... - 0.999... so 9x = 9 and x = 1.

Third argument: the difference 1 - 0.999... is less than 10 to the minus n for every n. The only non-negative real with this property is 0. So 1 - 0.999... = 0 and 0.999... = 1.

Decimals are a representation, not an identity. Any real with a terminating decimal also has a 999...-style alternative: 0.5 = 0.4999..., 1 = 0.999..., 0.123 = 0.122999... The two representations are equal.

In educational settings this is one of the most strongly contested results — students often refuse to accept it. The objection is usually based on confusing representations with the numbers themselves.
items.why: Decimals feel like unique addresses for numbers. They are not — every terminating decimal has a recurring-9 twin, and equality of the two is logically forced.

items.title: The square root of 2 cannot be written as a fraction
items.claim: Diagonal of a unit square has length root 2. The Pythagoreans believed all lengths were ratios of whole numbers. Hippasus showed root 2 wasn't. Legend says the Pythagoreans drowned him for revealing it.
items.prompt: Sketch the proof that root 2 is irrational.

options.text: It has too many decimal places

Assume root 2 = a/b in lowest terms. Then 2b squared = a squared, so a is even (say a = 2c). Then 2b squared = 4c squared, so b squared = 2c squared, so b is even. But a and b were lowest terms — contradiction
Because computers can't store it exactly

items.reveal:
The Pythagorean brotherhood (c. 500 BC) believed numbers were the foundation of reality and that all measurable lengths could be expressed as ratios of integers.

Hippasus of Metapontum supposedly proved the diagonal of a square is not commensurable with its side. Different ancient sources say he drowned at sea — some say by accident, some say murdered by his fellow Pythagoreans for exposing the result.

The proof: suppose root 2 equals a/b in lowest terms. Squaring: 2 = a squared over b squared, so 2 b squared equals a squared. Hence a squared is even, so a is even (say a = 2c). Substituting: 2 b squared = 4 c squared, so b squared = 2 c squared, so b squared is even, so b is even. Both a and b are even — contradiction with 'lowest terms'.

The discovery that not all numbers are rational was a major shock; the Greeks came to call these new quantities 'incommensurable'. Modern mathematics calls them irrationals — and there are vastly more of them than rationals.
items.why: Numbers feel like they should always be expressible as ratios. The very first geometric constructions reveal they're not.

items.title: A walker who halves their distance forever still reaches the wall
items.claim: Walk halfway to a wall. Then half of what's left. Then half again. Infinitely many steps — but the total distance is finite (the original distance), and the total time (if you halve your time at each step too) is also finite. Zeno's paradox resolved.

options.text: Infinity — there are infinitely many terms
Exactly 1. Geometric series with ratio r where |r| < 1 sums to a/(1-r); here a = 1/2 and r = 1/2, so sum = (1/2)/(1/2) = 1
Depends on how many terms you take

items.reveal:
A geometric series: a + ar + ar^2 + ar^3 + ... For |r| < 1, the sum is a/(1-r).

Proof: let S = a + ar + ar^2 + ... Then rS = ar + ar^2 + ar^3 + ... = S - a. So S - rS = a, giving S = a/(1-r).

Examples:
1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... = (1/2)/(1 - 1/2) = 1.
0.999... = 0.9 + 0.09 + 0.009 + ... = 0.9/(1 - 0.1) = 1.
1 + 1/3 + 1/9 + ... = 1/(1 - 1/3) = 3/2.

For |r| >= 1: the series diverges. 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + ... grows without bound.

Zeno's paradoxes resolved: Achilles catches the tortoise in finite time because the catching-up steps form a convergent series. Modern calculus formalises 'limit' and 'sum to infinity', tools Zeno did not have.

Applications:
- Compound interest formulas (sum of payment streams).
- Mortgage/loan calculations.
- Probability of getting heads eventually in repeated coin tosses.
- Resonance in physics (geometric series of wave reflections).
- Convergence of decimal expansions, power series, Taylor expansions.

Fermat, Newton, Leibniz, Cauchy, Weierstrass — the theory of convergent series was refined over centuries. By Weierstrass's epsilon-delta formalisation (1850s), 'infinite sum equals 1' had precise rigorous meaning.

Non-convergent series: harmonic 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + ... diverges (slowly, but to infinity). Conditional convergence (alternating series) raises subtle issues — Riemann showed you can rearrange a conditionally convergent series to sum to any value.
items.why: Infinite tasks seem impossible. They're not: infinite quantities can sum to finite values, given the right conditions. Calculus tamed Zeno's paradoxes and made motion mathematically describable.
